Glossary: Physical Internet: Physical Internet (PI) is an revolutionary paradigm aimed at the effective and seamless connection of global logistics systems and services to enable efficient, sustainable, and resilient global logistics and supply chain management. \\nPI-container: the processing unit of unitisation in the PI systems, including transport containers, handling containers, and packaging containers, with standardised and modular sizes compatible with one another. Physical Internet: an emerging paradigm for supply chain sustainability and resilience The Rise of PI The concept of the Physical Internet (PI) was first introduced around 2009 by Professor Benoit Montreuil, who drew inspiration from the front-page of The Economist in 2006 that introduced the term (Montreuil, 2011). Since then, it has been explored in the seminal articles as a breakthrough management paradigm to improve the efficiency ad sustainability of the global logistics and supply chains (Montreuil, 2011; Ballot et al., 2014). PI is conventionally defined as a global logistics system based on the openness and interconnection of logistics networks and services, by a standardised set of collaboration protocols, modular containers, and smart interfaces. In essence, the vision of PI advocates mimicking the transmission of data packet over digital internet for freight transport and logistics over the physical world. It envisions a future of logistics where receiving or sending goods just like receiving or sending text messages or e-mails. To achieve this, it is necessary to build a shared network that connects the current heterogeneous global or local logistics networks and services, just like what digital internet does.  As illustrated in Figure 1, logistics flows in traditional distribution networks are managed through direct Origin-Destination (O-D) shipments. Despite the independence of networks (as well as supply chains), supplier factories, warehouses, and distribution centres are often \\nclustered due to the similarity of strategies and operational constraints in all supply chains. Consequently, these distribution networks often overlap. The PI network proposes the use of routers (that could be consolidation centres, cross-docking platforms, or micro-hubs for Drop-and-Hook only) within each cluster to consolidate flows, like the topology of a Hub-and-Spoke network but designed for multi-supply chain and multi-flow coordination. Instead of direct O-D routes, flows can now be routed through routers within the PI network to enable further consolidation, modal shifting, and request exchanges to improve transport efficiency and reduce empty backhaul runs. \\n Figure 1. Comparing traditional overlapping distribution networks (left) and PI-based shared network (right) (Example of FMCG flows of two retailers in France), from (Ballot et al., 2014) In this setting, it is foreseeable that fundamental changes and evolutions will happen on the currently prevailing operations management models and best-practices. It is therefore crucial, on one hand, to enhance the universal interconnectivity and interoperability among systems and networks in global logistics and supply chains, and, on the other hand, to change the stakeholders’ mindset from competition to cooperate and coopetition (Pan et al., 2019a). Such changes and evolutions can already be observed in the recent research works and innovation projects. Over the past two decades, PI research has grown rapidly across both academia and industry (see recent reviews in Wu et al. (2024b) and Münch et al. (2023)). Flagship academic journals in the field have dedicated special issues to the PI concept (Kong et al., 2023; Pan et al., 2021a; Ballot et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2017), complemented by the annual International Physical Internet Conference (IPIC) since 20141. In practice, milestone research and industrial projects have explored PI applications in real world2.  Given the promising potential, strategic development and deployment roadmaps are being established globally. For instance, ALICE (Alliance for Logistics Innovation through Collaboration in Europe) in collaboration with academia and industry leaders have launched the first PI roadmap to guide the European logistics sector’s transformation. Similar roadmaps  1 https://www.pi.events 2 https://www.etp-logistics.eu/liaised-projects/ Overlapping NetworksPI-Network ofNetworks\\nhave since been developed or have emerged in other regions, including Japan3, Australia, China. As shown in Figure 2, the European PI roadmap proposes a five-axis, bottom-up strategy to achieve the PI scenario by 2040: (1) Logistics Nodes: focusing on functional design of PI-node and the intralogistics digitalisation and automation; (2) Logistics Networks: aiming at connecting the PI-nodes for smart freight routing with multimodality; (3) System of Logistics Networks: aiming at budling the seamless interconnectivity of logistics networks with high digital, physical and business interoperability; (4) Access and adoption: concentrating network scalability relying on easy entry- and exit-strategies for actors, and system-wide Plug & Play functions; (5) Governance: defining common rules of PI systems, for asset sharing, competition or conflict management, etc. For each axis, periodic milestone goals are explicitly defined.  \\n Figure 2. The Physical Internet Roadmap released by ALICE (Alliance for Logistics Innovation through Collaboration in Europe) The Potential of PI The potential of PI to streamline logistics processes for the efficiency, sustainability, and resilience of global logistics and supply chains has been extensively studied and validated by previous research. Freight transport has been a primary focus of these studies. Among the early research on quantitative metrics and qualitative assessments, Sarraj et al. (2014) demonstrate that shipper cooperation through PI may increase truck fill rates by 17%, improve the consolidation of multi-chain freight for multimodal transport, and result in up to a 60% reduction in CO2 emissions from freight transport, all while maintaining cost-effectiveness and service levels. These findings are substantiated through case studies in the fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) sector in France.  3 https://www.meti.go.jp/shingikai/mono_info_service/physical_internet/pdf/20220308_1.pdf  \\n\\nIn parallel with transport, PI has also the potential to foster new inventory management models and practices that are more dynamic and resilient, as exemplified by the PI-based distributed inventory model in Figure 3. Previous studies reveal that these PI-based inventory models can reduce total logistics costs by up to 35% while maintaining the same service level, primarily due to lower overall inventory levels compared to traditional tree-like distribution networks (Yang et al., 2017a). Furthermore, Yang et al. (2017b) assert that PI can significantly enhance supply chain resilience by enabling the interconnection of networks and facilitating dynamic operations management in inventory control, such as enhanced bilateral transshipments and dynamic multi-sourcing. \\n Figure 3. Comparing replenishment schemes in traditional tree-like networks (left) and PI-based interconnected networks (right) from (Pan et al., 2015) (WH-warehouse, PoS-Point of sale, DC-Distribution centre, R-Retailer, S-Supplier) While early research on the PI primarily focused on proof-of-concept stage, the recent research landscape has shifted toward development and deployment. A central question is how the application of PI can effectively transform the nature of collaboration and operations in real-world businesses in logistics and supply chain. To achieve this, new managerial and decision-making tools that harness the advantages of this innovative paradigm are being investigated jointly by the researchers in the fields of PI and operations management. Operations management with PI The expanding body of literature on the PI has highlighted its potential as a vital enabler and driver of innovative operations management (OM) models in logistics and supply chain management (LSCM). This section examines the primary OM problems through the lens of PI (see Table 1), aiming to provide a comprehensive understanding of the related challenges and opportunities. - Multimodal system design and assessment (Chargui et al., 2022); Distributed inventory management: Inventory can be distributed across shared warehouses within PI network to support dynamic and resilient inventory policies. - Problem definition and modelling (Pan et al., 2015); - PI resiliency inventory models (Yang et al., 2017b); Revenue management in service procurement: PI introduces dynamic and cooperative environments for service providers to enhance their pricing and revenue management capabilities. - PI dynamic pricing (Qiao et al., 2019); - Blockchain and Smart Contracts in PI service procurement (Henry et al., 2022); - CPI pricing and revenue allocation mechanisms (He et al., 2024); Table 1. Examples of PI-related operations management PI-containers The PI paradigm emphasises the unitisation with standardisation and modularisation of processing and handling logistics units, referred to as PI-containers, as first introduced in the seminal work by Montreuil (2011). PI-containers are fundamental to PI systems, as they aim to enhance efficiency and interoperability in logistics by facilitating seamless service sharing and optimised handling and processing. If the maritime container is seen as a breakthrough innovation that revolutionised the maritime transport industry, PI-containers represent more of a reproduction in land transport. However, they should be able to adapt to different constraints and operational requirements. One crucial feature is that PI-containers should come in various typologies to meet different logistics needs, such as transport containers for carriers’ transport operations, handling containers for warehousing and sorting operations, or packaging containers for shippers’ production operations in factory (Montreuil et al., 2016). Since all these types should be modular and standardised, handling equipment can also be standardised to achieve economies of scope, as demonstrated by maritime ports.  Additionally, as Returnable Transport Items (RTIs), PI-containers should be reusable and returnable. This could help reduce the heavy use of cardboard boxes, thus improving overall sustainability of the sector. PI-containers may also be equipped with IoT devices to capture real-time transport data (Sallez et al., 2016). The data collected can provide shippers with end-to-end visibility and traceability of the goods within the PI-containers, and provide carriers with real-time transport information for freight re-routing. Some recent research also argue \\nthat PI containers may help reduce cargo theft in road transport (Gastón Cedillo-Campos et al., 2024) In practice, prototype development and industrial pilots are underway worldwide, such as the SMART Box4 in Europe. More innovations are expected. Freight routing protocols In the digital internet, data packets are routed via routers that determine the next hop(s) for incoming data packets using routing protocols such as TCP/IP, while considering real-time factors like network congestion and router failures. This decentralised decision-making process has proven highly reliable, efficient and effective for interconnecting large-scale, heterogeneous digital networks. Likewise, in PI network, freight (encapsulated in PI-containers) should be transported from the source to the destination, passing through PI nodes for consolidation and modal shifting. This is known as the PI freight routing problem, as first introduced in Sarraj et al. (2014). In traditional distribution networks, a company may design end-to-end routing plans using its own capacity, which can be known and managed in advance. This is called centralised planning. In the PI network, however, companies may share capacity and services, which introduces two major challenges to centralised planning approach. First, centralised planning requires complete information on capacity, which is very difficult to obtain in large-scale, multi-actor networks like PI, not to mention data privacy concerns. Second, while centralised planning has proven to be efficient, they often lack flexibility and resilience, as real-time information and disruptions are difficult to foresee in the models. Moreover, data or information privacy is also a critical issue related to centralised planning. To leverage the dynamics of PI, recent research tends to propose decentralised planning approaches, where routing is optimised at the level of hubs, much like the internet. Freight routing protocols have been developed for this purpose, such as the carrier-led cooperation protocol (Lafkihi et al., 2020), node-led carrier payment-incentivised protocol (Briand et al., 2022), resilient transport protocol (Achamrah et al., 2024), or privacy-protecting routing protocol (Sun et al., 2024). Synchro-modal transport Synchromodal transport, or synchromodality, is an advanced evolution of multimodal transport which is a concept that involves using at least two different transport modes to provide end-to-end services. This approach has gained attention as a cost-effective and environmentally sustainable solution, aligning with the European Union’s objective to achieve climate neutrality by 2050. Synchromodality distinguishes itself by leveraging real-time information, such as operational disruptions, available transport capacities, and specific shipper requirements, to enable seamless, dynamic modal shifts. This capability improves both the efficiency and reliability of transport services, allowing for the flexible re-routing of logistics units across multiple modes of transport. Ambra et al., (2019) was among the first to recognise the PI as a critical enabler for synchromodality. For a recent review on this topic, we refer to Sakti et al. (2023). At the level of logistics units, PI-containers offer enhanced (physical) interoperability across various transport modes, facilitating efficient modal shifts. Moreover, the real-time data provided by  4https://www.gs1belu.org/sites/gs1belu/files/2021-04/GS1%20Innovation%20Café%20GS1%20SMART-Box.pdf \\nPI-containers can reduce uncertainties, such as deviations in Estimated Time of Arrival (ETA), streamlining synchronisation process across the transport plans. In the context of this research, stochastic and robust optimisation methods are frequently applied to model these uncertainties. At the network level, synchromodality leverages the robust interconnection and sharing of multimodal transport service networks, which supports flow consolidation and transport coordination. This results in increased flexibility, economic benefits of scale and scope, and overall enhanced network efficiency. Critical decision-making considerations include freight re-routing strategies that weigh multiple objectives, encompassing resilience, environmental impact, cost-efficiency, and service quality. Besides, recent research has suggested applying synchromodality with PI to urban freight, aiming to leverage public transport for urban freight distribution and enhance sustainability (Labarthe et al., 2024). This initiative has been developed within the framework of hyperconnected city logistics based on PI systems (Crainic et al., 2023). Material handling and cross-docking While the PI draws conceptual inspiration from the digital internet, its intra-site (within PI nodes) material handling challenges are significantly more complex due to the involvement of physical objects. In PI cross-docking centres, whether single- or multimodal, PI-containers are unloaded from inbound transport, sorted, and then loaded onto outbound transport, as the example shown in Figure 4. The standardisation of PI containers facilitates high levels of automation in these operations, enhancing both efficiency and speed (Montreuil et al., 2010). An illustrative example is found in modern maritime port operations, where standardised logistics units (e.g., maritime containers) and handling equipment (e.g., port cranes) enable significant automation, such as the deployment of automated guided vehicles (AGVs) for intra-terminal container movement. The PI framework is heavily inspired by such successful examples. Recently, there has been growing focus on designing automated PI-container sorting systems, particularly to optimise cost and energy efficiency in multimodal cross-docking centres (Chargui et al., 2022). \\n Figure 4. Example of PI cross-docking centres, from (Chargui et al., 2022) \\n\\nDistributed inventory management In parallel with transport, the PI paradigm also offers a promising approach for developing more effective and resilient policies and models in inventory management. PI establishes an interconnected network that facilitates warehouse capacity sharing, enabling inventory spread across shared facilities closer to consumer markets. This approach allows for dynamic sourcing through bilateral transshipments between warehouses, fostering flexible multi-sourcing strategies. In this framework, key inventory management decisions, such as sourcing location, order timing, and order quantity, are optimised for each order based on real-time data (e.g., inventory levels at nearby warehouses, available transport capacity). Similar to the transport protocols, inventory control in the PI framework can also rely on protocol-based management rather than centralised optimisation models, which enhances flexibility and responsiveness (Pan et al., 2015). Recent startups, such as Flexe and Spacefill, have increasingly focused on distributed inventory models. Initially, these companies operated primarily as matching platforms for warehouse capacity, listing available space in partner warehouses for clients seeking additional on-demand storage capacity. This model allows companies greater flexibility to adapt to fluctuations of storage demands. As a result, these solutions enable companies to reconsider traditional strategies related to inventory location, replenishment schemes, and capacity management, especially compared to in-house-only warehousing models. Revenue management in service procurement To maintain reliability and incentivise participation, PI should prioritise both logistics efficiency and the engagement of service providers. Within PI nodes, two types of service requests need to be effectively allocated to providers (carriers): new requests from shippers and in-transit requests from carriers seeking to subcontract shipments already in hand. These requests predominantly consist of less-than-truckload (LTL) volumes across various transport modalities. This setting offers carriers higher flexibility and agility in managing capacity management and fleet. Innovative OM models can therefore be designed to enhance carriers’ operational efficiency and revenue. Examples include dynamic LTL pricing models informed by real-time demand forecasting and capacity supply (Qiao et al., 2020), as well as Blockchain and Smart Contract solutions to streamline and automate the transport service procurement process within PI hubs (Henry et al., 2022). The PI framework promotes mutual resource sharing, enabling carriers to benefit economies of scale and scope. In freight transport, economies of scale typically involve (multi-shipper) freight consolidation, leading to higher shipment volumes and reduced per-unit transport costs. Meanwhile, economies of scope are realised through carrier lane exchanges, which minimise empty runs (Pan et al., 2019a). However, determining how to facilitate request exchanges is crucial to balance the interests of carriers and shippers alike. In this context, auction mechanisms have garnered significant attention (Xu et al., 2025). The use of serious gaming approaches, particularly those focused on auction platforms and cooperative rules, is emerging as a method to explore and understand the new opportunities and challenges PI presents for carriers (Lafkihi et al., 2025). \\nTransformative impact of PI on Supply Chain and Operations Management As PI continues to develop and expand, it is expected to pose significant challenges to existing operations management (OM) models and best practices. This disruption will likely drive companies to accelerate innovation, particularly in digitalisation and sustainable transformation. The transformative impact of PI can be analysed through the following pathways. Towards cooperative operations management Collaboration in PI A pivotal role of PI is to coordinate logistics flows and services among heterogeneous networks of multiple parties for mutual benefit. This includes both traditional vertical collaboration in supply-client relationships and horizontal collaboration between parties at the same level of the supply chain, such as shippers collaboration, carriers collaboration (Pan et al., 2019a). The former has been well-studied since the advent of SCM in the early 1980s; however, the latter has only recently gained attention. Since then, the term cooperative competition, or simply coopetition, has been increasingly used to describe the relationship of “cooperation while in competition” between two parties, whether vertical or horizontal, in supply chains (see a recent review in Katsaliaki et al. (2024)). Recently, the theory of the Sharing Economy has further established a foundation for such mutual collaboration for resources sharing and logistics operations, for example truck sharing, or requests exchange (Gansterer et al., 2022). Incentives The impact of the coopetition paradigm in LSCM is still unfolding. One of the primary questions to address is the incentives for coopetition, that is, why competitors should collaborate to share resources and services (Katsaliaki et al., 2024). This question is particularly important in PI comprising both vertical and horizontal collaboration, with the latter often presenting harder barriers and challenges. Co-creation and sharing of value among collaborators are more critical than ever. While the aforementioned research has demonstrated PI’s potential in creating overall and mutual benefits, the issue of value sharing remains challenge (Pan et al., 2019a).  Early PI-focused studies propose using Collaborative Game Theory approaches, like the Shapley value, coalition formation with stable gain sharing rules (Barbarino and Boute, 2023). While these approaches may be effective in small-scale collaborations, critical limitations are foreseeable in large-scale cases like PI, due to the complexity and dynamic nature of such collaborative systems. Recent research suggest that PI may function with collaborative rules that are explicitly defined at the level of network, to ensure the incentives of both shippers and service providers (Lafkihi et al. 2020). Based on the rules, carriers can exchange on-hand requests to enhance capacity management and increase revenue without harming the interests of shippers. The design of such rules can be related to the research of mechanism design theory.  \\nDigital transformation by PI Digital interoperability As an innovative paradigm, PI embraces cutting-edge digitalisation technologies to accelerate digital transformation in LSCM. Early PI development focused primarily on interconnecting and standardising heterogeneous information systems across enterprises and supply chains to enhance the digital interoperability (Pan et al., 2021b). Notable initiatives, such as the European projects FENIX5 or FEDeRATED6, aim to establish a federated digital network for seamless logistics information exchange. A range of technologies, including ontology and semantics, application programming interfaces (APIs), blockchain technologies, have been explored to enhance digital interoperability across diverse information systems. This digital infrastructure is expected to support essential PI functionalities, most importantly, PI-containers and freight traceability, end-to-end logistics visibility, and information sharing for collaborative transport planning and resource management.  Towards Cyber-physical Internet Building upon interoperable digital infrastructure, recent research proposes the integration of Digital Twin and Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) technologies to advance PI towards the next stage: the Cyber-Physical Internet (CPI), a concept firstly coined by Professor George Q. Huang in the theme-based project SynchroHub (Wu et al., 2024a). Figure 5 illustrates the organisation framework of logistics operations in CPI. Inspired by the TCP/IP architecture, CPI suggests five layers specifically adapted for transport and logistics operations: infrastructure, link, network, transport, and application. The network topology mirrors that of the digital Internet, resembling a structure of (sending) host-router-host (receiving). In this configuration, freight transport and routing are guided by routing tables that specify each hop for the freight (defined as standardised shipment units, a.k.a. PI-containers) at the router level. Moreover, CPI comprises three types of network configuration to facility the interconnection of networks: Local Area Network (LAN) and Catchment Area Network (CAN) to consolidate and coordinate local logistics facilities and assets, and Wide Area Network (WAN) that connects LANs for network-wide collaboration. While PI emphasises the openness and interconnection of logistics services and systems, CPI focuses on integrating and synchronising physical and digital networks to enhance the adaptability, efficiency, sustainability, and resilience of logistics operations. In CPI, Digital Twin technology plays a central role by linking the physical and digital worlds, enabling comprehensive system monitoring and situational awareness. This integration further allows data analytics and artificial intelligence to contribute more effectively to decision-making processes based on online or offline data. Promising research avenues are currently being investigated, including online contextual learning to mitigate uncertainties in logistics, innovative approaches to pricing and revenue management within CPI, and the design and optimisation of online freight routing protocols (He et al., 2024).   5 fenix-network.eu 6 www.federatedplatforms.eu \\n Figure 5. Illustration of logistics operations in CPI, from (Wu et al., 2024b) AI-empowered PI The rise of Artificial Intelligence, particularly Machine Learning (ML), Large Language Model (LLM) and Generative AI (GenAI), and more recently AI agents, is expected to significantly enhance LSCM by streamlining logistics processes and improving productivity. The PI (as well as CPI) provides a foundational structure that allows AI to reach its full potential within this field. On one hand, PI enhances data interoperability and standardisation, enabling AI models to access consistent, high-quality and interoperable datasets. This improved data quality and sourcing boosts the accuracy and reliability of AI analytics for demand forecasting, optimisation of operations across logistics operations, and so on. On the other hand, PI promotes modular, plug-and-play logistics systems, making it an ideal application field for GenAI-driven knowledge management and AI agents-based autonomous decision-making. GenAI may facilitate the seamless integration of systems and infrastructure, allowing for greater flexibility and adaptability in rapidly evolving logistics environments. Then, decision makers can be effectively and efficiently aided by AI agent technologies. Innovations on business models Platform-based and service-oriented models Logistics as a Service (LaaS), akin to the Mobility-as-a-Service (MaaS) model, has emerged as an innovative, customer-centric approach within the logistics industry, serving both business-to-consumer (B2C) and business-to-business (B2B) markets. The LaaS model rely on digital platforms as integrative interfaces that consolidate diverse logistics services. These demand-supply matching platforms provide flexible and adaptable solutions tailored to the specific needs of shippers and consumers (Beckers et al., 2023). This model includes innovations such as digital logistics marketplaces, such as crowdsourcing platforms and freight-matching or exchange platforms, which represent a new type of stakeholder in the logistics ecosystem. \\n\\nThese platforms typically operate asset-light or asset-free, utilising business models based on one-time contracts (or on-demand services), in contrast to traditional logistics providers who rely on fixed-term contracts spanning one or more years with the clients. By dynamically managing logistics capacity and expertise, LaaS platforms adopt a service-oriented approach that enhances service quality and value for clients, marking a shift from traditional asset-based third-party logistics (3PL) models, which primarily focus on maximising asset utilisation and productivity (Pan et al., 2019b). LaaS with PI The PI and LaaS have the great potential to complement each other in creating a more efficient, flexible, and customer-centred logistics ecosystem. PI’s principles of resource and service sharing align well with LaaS’s platform-driven approach, positioning it as a potential coordinator for multi-actor flows and operations. In this way, LaaS platforms may complement other intermediaries in PI like 4PL, trustee, and freight control tower, enhancing their service orientation. Moreover, by integrating with the PI system’s plug-and-play functions, LaaS can support greater network scalability. Conversely, LaaS platforms can exploit the range of logistics services within PI to offer enhanced flexibility and customer experience to the clients. Practical examples are emerging, particularly in the FMCG sector, for instance, European urban logistics projects such as ULaaDS (ulaads.eu) and LEAD (leadproject.eu). Conclusion and takeaways Conclusion The Physical Internet (PI) is a relatively new logistics paradigm with a history spanning just over 15 years. It has undergone rapid development, progressing from initial conceptualisation and proof-of-concept to its current stage of deployment. This paradigm aligns seamlessly with ongoing innovations aimed at digital and sustainable transformation in global logistics and supply chain. In this context, this chapter explores the significant opportunities and challenges that PI introduces to current Operations Management (OM) models, as well as the key pathways for transformative change. It suggests that PI has the potential to fundamentally reshape OM models and best practices across various logistics operations, including packaging, material handling, transportation and inventory management, and service provider’s revenue management. To capitalise on the opportunities presented by this paradigm shift, companies are encouraged to develop innovative models and practices tailored to the evolving logistics landscape. Takeaways for logistics and supply chain operations managers This chapter provides operations managers with practical and innovative insights into global logistics and supply chain management (GLSM). From the perspectives of PI, it reveals the importance for firms to proactively address evolving global standardisation designed to enhance inter-firm interoperability across both physical and digital aspects. Especially, the early adoption of digital transformation initiatives, combined with adherence to standardisation practices, can significantly strengthen a company’s capacity for international collaboration and competitiveness within the logistics and supply chain sectors. Furthermore, the chapter underscores the necessity of a paradigm shift in managerial mindsets toward horizontal collaboration and coopetition. New coopetition paradigms and practices, notably the PI paradigm, are emerging as new norms to unlock synergies across supply chains. Lastly, operations managers should prepare for the transformative impact of digitalisation on traditional decision-making models and tools used in operations management. The integration of Data Science and Digital Twins technologies into decision-making processes is expected to fundamentally enhance both operational and strategic decision-making capabilities. These advancements hold the potential to significantly improve overall supply chain performance, particularly in dynamic, complex, and increasingly collaborative global environments. Takeaways for OM/OR researchers OM/OR researchers in the field of GLSM can leverage PI to drive innovation in OM/OR models and processes, such as collaborative joint planning, dynamic pricing of services, and distributed inventory management, in either deterministic or uncertain environments.
